## PUBLIC COMMENT

1. The Mayor advised that the purpose of the public comment session is to give residents of Manchester the opportunity to address the Board. All people wishing to speak must sign up with their name, address and topic. Once called, they will have up to three minutes to speak and any comments must be directed to the chair and concluded when their time is up. If the Clerk calls their name and they are not present to speak, they will not be given a second opportunity. Any resident wishing to speak will come forward to the nearest microphone, clearly state their name and address when recognized and give their comments.

**Troy Micklon, 29 Ode Way:** At the last few meetings, I've raised some observations regarding how the city addresses snow emergencies here in Manchester. In doing so, several residents have reached out to me about winter operations more broadly. One recurring concern that they've raised is sidewalk snow removal, and the confusion over who is responsible for clearing municipal sidewalks. Recently, I reviewed a number of the SeeClickFix responses regarding snow removal from sidewalks and Ordinance 150.061 was cited, which states that property owners are responsible for maintaining sidewalks free of snow and ice. At the same time, New Hampshire law provides that sidewalks constructed as part of the public highway system are maintained by the municipalities. RSA 231:113 states that such sidewalks shall be maintained by the city or town in which they are located. Additionally, the New Hampshire Supreme Court in State versus Jackman, all the way back from 1898, recognizes that municipalities cannot fully shift their statutory sidewalk maintenance duties onto abutting properties. More recently in Tinker versus Tilton, the court clarified that municipal sidewalks must be maintained in an accessible condition, including reasonable snow removal by the cities. Rather than simply raising this issue, I've included two possible ordinance updates in the handout, which I have for you tonight. First, the board could simply strike the reference to sidewalks from 150.061 entirely so that the ordinance applies only to walkways, steps, and driveways located on private property. And second, the board could clarify that 150.061 applies only to private sidewalks located on the property, and ensuring that ordinances do not create confusion with municipal sidewalks located on the public right of way. Both approaches are intended to bring the ordinance into clear alignment with state law, while still preserving reasonable expectations for property owners to maintain features on their property, regardless of how the city ultimately proceeds. I would suggest that any responses regarding sidewalk snow removal, whether through SeeClickFix or any other public communications, clearly reflect the distinction between municipal sidewalks within the public right of way and private walkways located on private property. Providing that clarity will help ensure residents understand both the city's responsibilities and their own while keeping our ordinances and state law aligned.

**Rick Blais, Chestnut Street:** Before I get started, I just want to make a note. There's a young lady that was supposed to do the Pledge of Allegiance, and I think it got missed, so maybe you can address that later on. Congratulations to all the winners from the election. I am back in New Hampshire, glad to bring back the snow with me. For more than two decades now, the Manchester School District has struggled to deliver the level of education our children deserve. This is not a political rooted statement. It's rooted in decades of declining results. The state keeps all the records. Year after year, we see reports showing significant proficiency scores, widening achievement gaps, and just slipping away. Students graduate without the skills they need to compete in today's economy. Meanwhile, families are told the answer is always the same: more money. This year alone, we're being asked for another ten plus million dollars. I don't know what the last number was, but let's be clear, investing in education is important. I fully support paying great teachers well, providing safe schools, giving students the tools they need. But investing without accountability is not leadership. It's complacency. And that's what I've seen for 20 years. I am a graduate of Central High. I mean, even back then, you saw that starting to creep into the school systems. For over 20 years, spending has risen, administrative costs have exploded out of control. Not the teacher's costs, but the administration costs. Budgets have expanded. Yet the outcomes have no meaningful improvement on the kids. If a private business delivered mediocre results 20 years, while increasing budgets year over year, leadership would change, strategies would change, systems would change. Why is it different in education? This is not about attacking teachers. Many of them work tirelessly late nights with kids, doing homework, reports, all kinds of things. This is about priorities and accountability. We need to ask tough questions. Where is the money actually going? Why are reading and math proficiencies not where they should be? And if you're an employer, you know what I'm talking about in interviews with some of these people. Oh my God, I feel bad for them. Why are families increasingly seeking alternatives? We hear so much about charter schools and if we're going to invest in our schools, it doesn't have to be money. It has to be standards. If you don't have standards that kids can achieve, it's not worth putting it out there for anybody, money-wise. Why does more funding automatically mean better results? You know, every time we have a budget issue, the kids are marched in from schools, parents are marched in. More money. More money. You're taking money away. This is a budget. It's not even approved yet. You're not taking anything away. But you as aldermen and mayor, you guys are asking for accountability and you get toasted for that. Unfortunately, throwing money at a problem without structural reform is not a solution. It's a delay tactic. We need results driven approaches, clear performance benchmarks, transparent budget, administrative efficiencies, especially with AI now, strong support for the classroom teachers, data backed curriculum for improvements, and leadership that is accountable to the parents and taxpayers. Our children get one chance at their education, one chance to learn to read proficiently, one chance to build math foundations, one chance to develop the discipline and skills that shape their future. We owe them an excellent education, not a good enough education to skirt them by. We owe them results, not excuses. And we pay. We, the taxpayers, want transparency. I don't think any of us here want to deny a child a great education, but when we see our money being squandered on stupid projects, we get upset. This isn't about cutting education, it's about demanding performance. It's about aligning funds with measurable improvements. It's about restoring trust. Manchester families deserve schools that prepare their children for college, careers, and in life, not a system that asks more every year while delivering the same outcome. It's time for a reset. It's accountability, and it's time to put the students, not the bureaucracy first. I got my little form to fill out for my commercial building that says, hey, what size is it? All I can say is, does this mean we're going to be paying? You're going to tell me that my tax rate went down and I should be grateful. But yet I'm paying $5,000 more. It doesn't make any sense. So, I would encourage you, don't play the game with the new assessments that are coming out. A dollar is a dollar. But I appreciate all you guys do. And thank you again for volunteering your time.

**Mayor Ruais:** May I suspend this public comment period for one second? I need to apologize. We had a scheduling mishap. I would love to invite the kids from Saint Catherine's to come on up and do the Pledge of Allegiance. Why don't we have you come and say your names in the microphone? Tell the audience who you are and then we'll do the pledge.

**Cindy Stewart, 255 Sagamore Street:** I am a member of the Manchester School Board. As we continue deliberating the fiscal year 27 budget, I want to clarify some facts and correct some misinformation. The school board has approved three operating budgets. First, the required tax cap compliant budget, which creates a $16 million shortfall from our current operating budget. Second, a baseline budget that simply level funds the district so that we can maintain current staffing and programs. And third, a fully funded budget that moves Manchester closer to the state average for per pupil spending. Right now, Manchester spends about $4,600 less than the state average. Our current situation is a result of chronic underfunding, rising mandated expenses, downshifted state costs, and the requirement that we provide transportation and special education services to parochial, private, and charter school students with no reimbursement. These pressures come from federal, state, and city levels. I want to share my understanding on how the tax cap works. It applies to both revenue and expenses, and the combined city and school budgets cannot exceed it without an override from you, the Board of Mayor and Aldermen. The tax cap is essentially meant to function as an annual cost of living adjustment. So, when people say the school district has been under the tax cap since 2021, thinking that's a good thing, what that really means is that the district has not received a cost-of-living adjustment for six straight years. If we had received a full tax cap compliant budget in the last two fiscal years, we would likely not be facing this $16 million shortfall. I've heard claims that the district is asking for a 9% or a 14% tax increase. Those numbers are simply not confirmed, as the actual tax impact depends entirely on how revenue is allocated between city services and the school district. We will not know that information with certainty until Mayor Ruais presents his budget at the end of this month. Finally, I want to address the idea that the district has too much fat. We are a $265 million enterprise, serving 12,000 students with 2,350 staff members, and we only have six administrators. We are the largest and most complex district in the state. 24% of our students receive special education services, 21% are English language learners, and 54% are economically disadvantaged. This district is run efficiently and responsibly. During my campaign, I knocked on hundreds of doors. The overwhelming majority of residents that I met told me that they want our public schools to be made whole. They understand that investing in our schools is an investment in our future workforce and in the community. Leaders sitting in our classrooms today and Manchester can only thrive when our public schools are strengthened, protected and celebrated.

**Garth Corriveau, 215 North Street:** I'm a former Manchester Alderman, having represented ward six for six years. I'm here in my capacity as an attorney with Devine Millimet representing Project Elm LLC. Project Elm owns a five-story building which includes the Campo Enoteca and Taj India restaurants, located at 959 and 967 Elm Street in the central business district. Project Elm purchased the premises from North Street Properties, LLC, following approval by the Board of Mayor and Aldermen of North Street's 79-E Community Revitalization application on April 16th, 2020, for a required covenant between the city and North Street. However, it was never recorded by the city prior to the sale of the premises to Project Elm. Rather than record the covenant, city staff notified us that a new 79-E application must be filed due to changes in the redevelopment project, namely the conversion of vacant office space into 27 residential units, rather than the initially proposed 36 units. Accordingly, my client submitted its 79-E application to the city on January 16th, 2026. Attached to my testimony, which I provided to the City Clerk, is a letter to the BMA from my colleague, Attorney Suzanne Brunelle, containing additional factual and legal details about our 79-E application that I would encourage you to read tonight, because tonight you are scheduled to vote on the implementation of a TIF district for the purpose of constructing a parking garage on the Pearl Street lot. Although 959-967 Elm Street is located within the proposed TIF district, we want to be transparent that Project Elm is not seeking duplicative public financing, but simply the same relief granted by this board less than two years ago. For reasons unknown to us, our January 16 79-E application was not placed on tonight's BMA agenda, despite it having been submitted prior to the BMA's February 3rd public hearing on the TIF district, and to the letter in your agenda from Community and Development Director Jeffrey Belanger, to effectuate the adoption of the TIF district dated February 24th. Yet this board apparently will vote on the TIF district before voting on my client's 79-E application. The BMA is not scheduled to vote on my client's application until March 17th. But you are being asked to approve the TIF district tonight; when you decide to schedule votes on these separate matters is a policy choice of this board. But in recognition of the past 79-E approval of this redevelopment project by this board and these unique scheduling circumstances beyond the control of my client, we request that the 79-E relief be granted or regranted, depending on your perspective at a fair hearing on March 17th, regardless of tonight's vote on adopting the TIF district.

**Avery Cyr, 30 Hanover Street:** I just wanted to take a moment to remember my former teacher Miss Gemme, she was my creative writing teacher, and she was a teacher to probably hundreds of students. She first started working for the district back in 2000. And she's been working up until her death last week. And I just want to say she was really somebody who filled the room, and she really connected well with all of her students. She really tried hard to teach the material, and she just was one of those teachers that went above and beyond. She was involved in a lot of activities. She was a senior class advisor. She was one of the coaches for cross country. She was the basketball coach. She helped design some yearbooks. And she was also part of the Central Pride Foundation. I interacted with her quite a bit when I was there at Central myself. And I just think that her loss is very shocking and will leave a really important personality. I think she's almost kind of become part of Central High School's identity. And I just think everyone's going to be really sad, and I'm going to be sad. And I just want to take one moment to remember her. The last thing I'll say is anybody who's interested, calling hours for her will be tomorrow from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m. at the Connor-Healy Funeral Home at 536 Union Street. And her funeral will be on Thursday, so two days from today at 10 a.m. at the Saint Catherine of Siena Church at 207 Hemlock Street. This is all in her publicly available obituary, so I'd assume it's for the public.

**Glenn Ouellette, 112 Auburn Street:** First, I want to thank our first responders. It's been a tough winter and a lot of accidents, a lot of snow. The highway department's done very well, especially with the amount of snow that we've had and we're still having. So, I congratulate them. There are some things in the city that really are working as they should be, and that is good. All cities have problems. That's for sure. Some greater than others. Education is an important thing to our community, for our students' future, but we also have to be accountable, just as we have to be accountable here at the board for the services that they are providing. That's the way it works. I want to thank the city for opening up the new shelter. It's going to take care of a lot of the seniors and handicapped that are losing their rent because of the new state law that provides that. It's changed it so much and it's their fault. If they only have a 3% increase in income through their Social Security, and that's all they have for income, and the rent goes up 15%, 20%, 30%, it doesn't compute. So, they're out the door. We can do better as a city. And we should. These people, most of them have worked all their lives. With that, I think we need to do better on some of the issues of the homeless. I understand that those who do not want to conform with the rules and regulations and laws, we are an abiding city, county, state and nation of laws. That is hard to help these people and sometimes you can't reach them. There are some things you can do to help people, and there are some things you can't. But most people that are homeless are looking for a way out. And I personally will tell you that people in this city that are becoming homeless are not dreaming to become homeless or they don't want it. It takes away their jobs. It takes away their lives. It's a big change to go from living in a home and being homeless, and it takes sometimes a long time, the detriment of what is caused to get these people back on board. So, whatever we can do to help those who want to help themselves, we should do it because that's to our benefit. And putting them back into working, paying taxes, volunteering, the things that we do as a community.

**Alderman Sapienza:** I'm looking at that chart there. It's a bit complex, but my understanding is at the end of January, $54 million has been spent on phase one so far. **Sharon Wickens, Finance Director:** So, the bond has been spent. We didn't go out and issue the full amount of the bond because we didn't need all of the funds immediately. So, we've been doing it in increments so that we're only spending interest on money that we expect to spend in that year.

**Alderman Sapienza:** Another way of putting it is none of the operating budget has been spent on phase one so far.

**S. Wickens:** The school district's operating budget, yes. **Alderman Sapienza:** So, $54 million expended so far in phase one, and $54 million has been spent from the operating budget to cover what they've spent.

**Alderman Sapienza:** $114 million so far.

*Minutes Prepared By: Michael Intranuovo*
headline: Approved a Pearl Street parking garage TIF district, multiple funding requests, and the consent agenda, while sending Hanover Street parking changes back to committee.
summary: The board heard public comments on sidewalk snow removal, school funding, education accountability, and other topics, then approved a tax increment financing district for a parking garage on the Pearl Street Lot. It adopted the consent agenda, approved several grant and funding requests including $65,000 in opioid abatement funds for Squad One and three fire department grant applications, approved parking signage changes for a developer, and confirmed an appointment to the Arts Commission. It also pulled a Hanover Street parking regulation item off the table and referred it back to the Committee on Public Safety, Health & Traffic for further work.
decisions: Approved the consent agenda, including acceptance of the February 17 BMA and Finance minutes and approval of a sidewalk petition for 152 Poplar Street.
Accepted the Revolving Loan Fund update, unanimous vote.
Accepted Finance Department reports on accounts receivable over 90 days, aging, and outstanding receivables, unanimous vote.
Accepted the Monthly Financial Report (unaudited) for the first seven months of fiscal year 2026, unanimous vote.
Approved and referred to the Committee on Bills on Second Reading a non-lapsing Welfare Reserve Account, unanimous vote.
Approved increasing the Disabled Veteran Credit from $2,000 to $2,500 effective April 1, 2026, unanimous vote.
Received and filed a proposal to amend Rule 3 regarding public participation, 3-2 vote (Fajardo, Bonilla, Kaw-uh voted yea; Kantor and Sapienza voted nay).
Received and filed a request to install a mural on the Victory Parking Garage, unanimous vote.
Approved a mural at the Canal Street and Pleasant Street crossing, unanimous vote.
Approved a revocable license agreement for a structure at 290 Granite Street partially within the city's right of way, unanimous vote.
Authorized Dube Dogs to operate a food service cart at the Mill Girl steps location for five years at $500 per year, unanimous vote.
Accepted the Joint School Buildings Committee report on Manchester School District Priority I status and financial reports for December 2025 and January 2026.
Laid over nominations for the Board of Adjustment, Planning Board, Manchester Public Television Service, and Retirement Board until the next meeting, per Rule 23.
Laid over aldermanic nominations for the Manchester Public Television Service until the next meeting, per Rule 23.
